summary: Instagram is carrying the channel: most videos get 1,000+ views there, while YouTube Shorts mostly gets under 60 views. The best performers are short 'X doesn't do what you think, it does Y' explainers about common robot and sensor projects (gyro robot, clap switch, line follower), which also get the most likes and saves. Weak spots are generic 'How does X work?' question titles, plain everyday-device topics (lift, tap, smoke alarm), and videos posted to only one platform.
winningPattern: Hindi, Instagram-first. Subject is a hands-on maker project or module (robot, clap switch, DHT11, mic) that viewers can build. Hook is a surprising contradiction: 'X can't do the obvious thing, it only does Y' or 'without Z the robot falls'. Titles are short, punchy Hinglish with one emoji, no jargon. Clap switch and robot-balance videos also did well on YouTube (500-680 views), so relatable, build-it-yourself topics work on both platforms.
doMore: Make robot and maker-project videos (balancing, line follower, obstacle avoidance) with a 'without this part it fails' hook
Use the 'doesn't do X, only does Y' title format, which beat plain 'How does X work?' titles
Post every video to both YouTube and Instagram; several videos have zero on one platform
Make follow-ups to winners, such as the clap switch series, with a new angle each time
End with a save or share prompt like 'save this for your next project', since saves and shares signal strong interest
stopDoing: Generic 'Kaise kaam karta hai?' titles on everyday devices like lift, tap, mall door, smoke alarm
Repeating the same topic with near-identical titles (several IR, tap, smoke, and clap videos overlap and compete)
Publishing English or single-platform videos that break the Hindi, both-platform routine
